question: A 16-year-old woman consulted for primary amenorrhea. It presents a normal female development of secondary sexual characteristics. The levels of estradiol and testosterone are normal. In the gynecological examination, agenesis of the vagina is appreciated. Ultrasound is performed and there is absence of uterus. The ovaries are normal ultrasound. No left kidney is seen. The most likely diagnosis is:
reasoning_chain: CHAIN: Absence of uterus + agenesis of the vagina -> Primary amenorrhea -> 90% CHAIN: Normal estradiol and testosterone levels + normal ovaries on ultrasound -> Exclusion of ovarian pathology -> 80% CHAIN: Absence of left kidney on ultrasound -> Suggestive of renal agenesis -> 70% CHAIN: Primary amenorrhea + agenesis of the vagina + absence of uterus -> Rokitansky syndrome -> 90%
enhanced_information: The most likely diagnosis for the 16-year-old woman with primary amenorrhea, absence of uterus, agenesis of the vagina, normal estradiol and testosterone levels, normal ovaries on ultrasound, and absence of left kidney is Rokitansky syndrome. This is supported by the presence of agenesis of the vagina and absence of uterus, which are characteristic features of Rokitansky syndrome.
analysis: The core medical principle here is the presence of primary amenorrhea, absence of uterus, agenesis of the vagina, normal estradiol and testosterone levels, normal ovaries on ultrasound, and absence of left kidney. These findings are classic for Rokitansky syndrome, also known as Mayer-Rokitansky-Küster-Hauser (MRKH) syndrome. This syndrome is characterized by Müllerian duct abnormalities resulting in the absence of the uterus and upper two-thirds of the vagina. The normal ovarian function distinguishes it from other conditions like Turner syndrome. The absence of the left kidney is a common associated anomaly in Rokitansky syndrome.
